Educational disclaimer

This book provides general gardening information. Plant needs vary by species, cultivar, climate, season, soil, and growing conditions. Product labels and local advice should be checked before applying fertilisers, pesticides, or other treatments. The author and publisher make no guarantee that every recommendation will suit every plant or location.
Safety note
Keep gardening products, sharp tools, and potentially toxic plants away from children and pets. Follow all product instructions and local rules.

Gardening is the practice of growing and caring for plants by understanding what they need. You do not need a large garden, expensive equipment, or years of experience. A sunny windowsill, a few containers, and a consistent routine are enough to begin.

items: Choose plants that suit your space, light, local climate, and routine.
Use a growing medium that holds moisture while allowing air to reach roots.
Water according to soil moisture and plant needs, not the calendar alone.
Recognise common signs of stress and respond carefully.
Create a simple maintenance routine that you can actually keep.

blocks.text: Start small and build confidence

Begin with two or three plants. Keep a small garden diary with the plant name, location, watering observations, and changes you notice. Small, steady habits teach you more than any single piece of advice, and every healthy leaf is proof that you are learning.
Choose one bright spot at home and put your first plants there. Seeing them every day makes you notice problems early.

title: Plan Your Garden Before You Buy

blocks.text: Observe your growing area at different times of day. Check direct sunlight, reflected heat, wind, rain exposure, access to water, and the amount of room available. A little observation before buying saves money and prevents disappointment.

items: Track sunlight in the morning, midday, and afternoon.
Measure the space and keep walkways clear.
Check drainage after rain.
Notice hot walls, strong drafts, and windy corners.
Decide how much time you can spend each week.

blocks.text: Match plants to real conditions
Choose plants for the conditions you have rather than forcing a plant to live in an unsuitable place. Ask a local nursery about varieties that perform well in your region and season.
Set a realistic budget
Start with healthy plants, a good potting mix, pots with drainage holes, and a few basic tools. Decorative extras can wait. A small, well-cared-for collection looks better than a crowded one.

blocks.text: How to pick a healthy plant

Look for firm stems, evenly coloured leaves, and new growth. Avoid plants with sticky leaves, webbing, spots, or a sour smell from the soil. Gently check that roots are not circling heavily at the bottom of the pot.
You can begin with a small, useful toolkit. Buy durable basics first; specialised tools can wait.

blocks.text: Keep your tools clean and sharp for better results and healthier plants. Wipe blades after use and dry them before storing.
Good soil provides nutrients, holds moisture, and allows air to reach the roots.
Soil components

items: Topsoil – nutrients and structure.
Compost – organic matter and microbes.
Sand – drainage and aeration.
Coco peat – moisture retention.

children.text: Mix roughly 2 parts garden soil, 1 part compost, and 1 part coco peat, adding a handful of coarse sand for drainage. For succulents and snake plants, use more sand.
pH measures how acidic or alkaline the soil is. Most vegetables, herbs, and flowers prefer slightly acidic to neutral soil. Inexpensive test kits are available at garden stores.

blocks.text: What to avoid
Meat, fish, dairy, oily foods, and pet waste attract pests and cause odours. Aim for roughly twice as much brown material as green.
Good compost = healthier plants + better soil. Finished compost looks dark and crumbly and smells earthy.

title: Watering Plants Correctly
tagline: The right amount, at the right time

blocks.text: Overwatering and underwatering are the most common mistakes. Learn to read the soil rather than following a rigid schedule.

items: Check soil moisture (top 2–3 cm).

Use room temperature water.
Ensure proper drainage.

blocks.text: The finger test

Push a finger about 2–3 cm into the soil. If it feels dry, water thoroughly until it drains from the bottom. If it feels damp, wait a day and check again. Succulents and snake plants prefer to dry out completely between waterings.

blocks.text: Observe changes early and adjust care before the problem grows.
Different plants need different light levels. Match each plant to the light it receives and it will need far less rescue later.
Reading the signs
Stretched, pale growth usually means too little light. Scorched, bleached patches suggest too much. Rotate pots a quarter turn each week for even growth.
Observe how plants respond and adjust placement if needed.

blocks.text: Heat and summer care

During North Indian summers, temperatures can exceed 40°C. Move delicate pots out of afternoon sun, group plants together to share humidity, water in the early morning, and use mulch to keep roots cooler.
Cold and winter care
Most tropical houseplants dislike temperatures below 10°C. Keep them away from cold windows at night, reduce watering, and avoid placing them near heaters or air-conditioning vents.
Wind
Wind dries leaves and soil quickly. On high balconies, use screens, heavy pots, and sturdy stakes for tall plants.
Humidity
Tropical plants such as ferns and calatheas appreciate higher humidity. Place pots on a tray of damp pebbles, and avoid misting at night to reduce fungal problems.

blocks.text: Signs of overfeeding
White crust on the soil surface, brown leaf tips, and sudden leaf drop. If this happens, flush the pot with plenty of clean water and pause feeding for a few weeks.

items: Use clean, sharp shears (wipe with rubbing alcohol).

blocks.text: Deadheading
Pinching off spent flowers encourages marigolds, petunias, and roses to keep blooming. Pinching the tips of basil and mint creates bushier plants.

Indoor plants improve the look and feel of your home and bring a sense of calm. Success depends mainly on light, so start by choosing plants for the brightest spot you have.
Indoor care essentials

items: Place plants within 1–2 metres of a bright window.
Water only when the top few centimetres of soil are dry.
Wipe leaves monthly and rotate pots weekly.
Keep plants away from air-conditioner and heater vents.
Use pots with drainage holes and empty saucers after watering.

blocks.text: Neem oil spray, soap water, and removing affected leaves help keep indoor plants healthy.

Check weight limits, avoid blocking drains, and secure pots against wind. Place saucers carefully so excess water does not drip onto neighbours below.

A good garden design is simple. Think about how you will use the space, how you will move through it, and what you want to see from your favourite window or seat.
Five simple design principles

items: Layers: tall plants at the back, medium in the middle, low at the front.
Repetition: repeat a few plants or colours for harmony.
Focal point: one standout pot, plant, or seating spot.
Pathways: leave room to walk and tend plants.
Odd numbers: groups of three or five look natural.

blocks.text: Mix foliage plants with flowering ones so colour lasts through the seasons. Use pots in a few matching shades or materials to keep a small space calm and tidy.

blocks.text: Q: How much sunlight do most plants need?
A: Most flowering and fruiting plants need 4–6 hours of direct sun. Foliage plants often do well in bright, indirect light.
Q: Can I grow vegetables in containers?
A: Yes. Many vegetables grow well in containers, including tomato, chilli, coriander, lettuce, and spinach. Use a pot at least 25–30 cm deep for larger plants.
Q: How often should I fertilise?
A: Generally every 2–4 weeks during active growth, using a diluted feed. Pause in extreme heat and winter dormancy.
Q: What is the best time to water?
A: Early morning or late evening, when water loss is lowest.
Q: Why are my plant leaves turning yellow?
A: Overwatering is the most common cause; also consider poor drainage, low light, or lack of nutrients.
Q: What is the best time to plant?
A: Early morning or evening, and in the right season for the plant, so that it can settle before extremes of weather.
